title: Drawing with Light
sub: Grades 5–8 · Science · Light, the negative and the print
objective: Students will discover that early photographs were made by light changing a light-sensitive surface: where most light fell, the paper darkened, so a camera made a **negative**, with light and dark the wrong way round. Laying that negative on fresh sensitive paper in the sun turned the tones back into a **print**. Students will reason about **exposure time** as a variable, and compare three Victorian processes — the daguerreotype, the calotype and wet collodion — by their materials and what each could do.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: A photograph is a chemical record of where light fell. The same reasoning — light in, a change out, one variable at a time — runs through every experiment you will design.

materials: The pictures on page 3, on screen or printed; the handouts, one per student; pencils
connection: **Visit the exhibition:** at the photography bench of the *Inventions Workshop,* make Talbot’s negative and print from it, sit for a daguerreotype in a head clamp, and match the three photographs to their processes. Poster 1 adds that in 1843 Anna Atkins began publishing the first book in Britain illustrated with photographs: blue “cyanotype” prints of seaweed, made by laying the plants on sun-sensitive paper.

steps.title: A strange window
script: Show Talbot’s window without naming it. Ask: *“What is strange about this picture of a window?”* Students notice that the panes, where daylight came in, are dark, and the stone bars light. Then tell them: this is the oldest known surviving paper negative, made by William Henry Fox Talbot of a window at Lacock Abbey, in August 1835.

screen.alt: A faded purple paper negative of a tall window: the panes come out dark and the stone bars between them light

steps.purpose: Notice that the oldest surviving negative has its light and dark reversed, before anything is explained.
students: What is strange about this picture of a window?
Where would the light have been brightest?

steps.title: Negative and print
script: **The model.** Inside the camera was paper that darkens in the light. Where the bright window shone on it, the paper darkened; where the dark stone was, little changed. So the negative has light and dark the wrong way round. A print was made by laying the negative directly on sensitized paper and putting it out in the sunlight: now the light passes through the pale parts of the negative and darkens the paper beneath, and the tones turn back. Talbot’s positive-negative process meant many prints could be made of the same image.

steps.title: Three ways
script: **Three ways.** Show the three photographs. The **daguerreotype** (announced by Louis Daguerre in 1839) was made on a silver-plated sheet; each was a single picture that could not be copied. Talbot’s **calotype** (patented 1841) used a sheet of good writing paper made sensitive to light with chemicals as its negative. In the **wet collodion** process (introduced in 1851 by F. Scott Archer) a glass plate was coated, exposed while still wet and developed at once; it gave very fine detail. Julia Margaret Cameron printed from such glass negatives.

**Hold still.** In the earliest days of the portrait daguerreotype, a photograph took over 15 minutes. That soon fell to just over a minute, but sitters still had to keep still the whole time, or the picture blurred; neck braces and head clamps were often used. Ask: *what variable did photographers want to shrink, and why?*

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout. Every level models a negative and a print on a grid; the Inventions Workshop’s exposure seconds appear as a game rule, never as real times.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Shade the negative of a simple window, then predict the print; match each process to its clue; finish a sentence on why sitters kept still.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Turn a scene into a negative and a negative back into a scene; plan a fair test of exposure time with its variables; choose a process for a job.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Explain the chain from light to print with a labeled model; reason from a single-print rule to a whole design; weigh exposure time against blur.

steps.purpose: Model the negative and the print, and reason about exposure time, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. Shade lightly in pencil: you may change your mind.

steps.title: The three compared
script: Project the comparison chart. Ask: *which process would you choose for a portrait to send to five relatives? Which for the finest detail? Which could never be copied?* Expect reasons that use the material: a negative on paper or glass makes copies possible; a silver plate does not.
